slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
On GitHub in 2026 that layer has two mechanisms that coexist: rulesets and classic branch protection rules.
This video covers what a rule is, what a ruleset is, how several of them combine, and who can skip them.

slides.body: And a point that surprises people who know classic protection: the Maintain role's documented right to push to protected branches does not apply to rulesets.
The textbook's analogy: a bank teller will move money between accounts for anyone with the right card, but checks each transfer against the account's conditions first …
The analogy breaks in one place: on GitHub the conditions are published, and anyone who can read the repository can read them.

lines.s: # pre-receive: the server runs this before any ref moves.
# Standard input has one line per proposed ref update: <old id> <new id> <ref name>
while read old new ref; do
refs/heads/main)                      # target of the branch rules
echo "rule 'restrict deletions': $ref may not be deleted"; status=1; continue
[ "$old" = "$zero" ] && continue    # creation: nothing to compare with
echo "rule 'block force pushes': the update would remove commits from $ref"; status=1
echo "rule 'require linear history': the update adds a merge commit to $ref"; status=1
refs/tags/v*)                         # target of the tag rules
echo "rule 'restrict deletions': $ref may not be deleted"; status=1
echo "rule 'restrict updates': $ref already exists and may not move"; status=1
# Install the rules on the server. Not executable yet: the "ruleset" exists but is disabled.
hint: The 'hooks/pre-receive' hook was ignored because it's not set as executable.
hint: You can disable this warning with `git config set advice.ignoredHook false`.

slides.body: The lab creates the ruleset from a JSON file kept in the course, through the REST API.
And if the ruleset is Active, it binds everyone at once, you included.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Believing --force-with-lease can get past a server rule. Root cause: both force options only switch off client-side checks; the rule is evaluated on the server.
Targeting feature* or release/* and assuming nested branch names are covered. Root cause: the star does not match a slash; a pattern that fails to match protects nothing and says nothing.
Loosening one ruleset and finding the merge still blocked. Root cause: all active rulesets and the classic rule are aggregated, and the most restrictive version of each rule applies.
Assuming administrators or the Maintain role can push past a ruleset. Root cause: under rulesets only the bypass list grants exceptions.
Leaving a ruleset disabled after an emergency. Root cause: a disabled ruleset enforces nothing and still appears in the settings page.

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: A rule is a server-side condition on a ref update: old ID, new ID, ref name.
Creation, deletion, force push, linear history and update restrictions need only those three values; reviews, checks and signatures need platform data.
A ruleset has a target, an enforcement status and a bypass list; * in a target does not cross a slash.
All applicable rulesets and the classic rule add up, and the strictest version of each rule holds.
Bypass leaves a trace; exemption does not; roles alone grant nothing under rulesets.

A ref is a name for a commit, such as a branch or a tag. Once you see a rule that way, "how did it get through" becomes a list of four things to check, in order. Hold on to the three questions. beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. The pull request chapter ended with a list of controls that are only advisory: a "changes requested" review, a red check, a CODEOWNERS file. This module is about the layer that makes them binding.

beats.text: On GitHub in 2026 that layer has two mechanisms that coexist: rulesets and classic branch protection rules. Most "why can't I merge" tickets come from not knowing that both are evaluated. beats.text: Rulesets. In one sentence: a ruleset is a named list of rules with three more things. A target: which refs. An enforcement status: on or off. And a bypass list: who is excepted. You can have up to 75 rulesets per repository, and 75 organization-wide rulesets.

beats.text: There are three kinds. A branch ruleset targets branches by name pattern, or "the default branch". A tag ruleset targets tags by name pattern. If the same rule is defined in different ways across the aggregated rulesets, the most restrictive version of the rule applies."
